news.Title: SanDisk (SNDK) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript
news.Content:
Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Thursday, Oct. 29, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Vice President of Investor Relations - Ivan Donaldson

Chairman and Chief Executive Officer - David V. Goeckeler

Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer - Luis Visoso

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator: Good afternoon, and welcome to Sandisk's First Quarter Fiscal Year 2027 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please also note today's event is being recorded. At this time, I'd like to turn the floor over to Ivan Donaldson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Ivan Donaldson: Before we begin, please note that today's discussion will contain forward-looking statements based on management's current assumptions and expectations, which are subject to various risks and uncertainties. These forward-looking statements include expectations for our technology and product portfolio, our business plans and performance, our capital allocation priorities, market trends and opportunities and our financial results. We assume no obligation to update these statements. Please refer to our annual report on Form 10-K and our other filings with the SEC for more information on the risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations. We will also make references to non-GAAP financial measures today.

Reconciliations between the non-GAAP and comparable GAAP financial measures are included in the written materials posted in the Investor Relations section of our website. With that, I'll turn the call over to David.

David V. Goeckeler: Thanks, Ivan. Good afternoon, and thank you for joining Sandisk's Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Earnings Call. We began fiscal year 2027 with another strong quarter, creating value for customers and shareholders and delivering results above guidance. Our strategy is working, and our execution is delivering strong results. Revenue for the quarter was $11 billion. Non-GAAP gross margin was 85.1% and non-GAAP earnings per share was $49.51. We generated $5.7 billion of adjusted free cash flow and returned $5 billion to shareholders through share repurchases. Our confidence in the long-term trajectory of the business is grounded in 3 enduring strengths: technology leadership, deep customer partnerships and disciplined financial management.

These strengths are reinforced by a structural increase in NAND demand, driven particularly by AI and by customer signals now extending beyond fiscal year 2030 through our new business models, our NBM partnerships. Together, they position us to invest with confidence in our technology road map, strengthen and expand our customer relationships, and deliver growing and durable free cash flow while returning capital to shareholders. It starts with our technology leadership. BiCS8 is the backbone of our current production portfolio and the industry benchmark for performance and density across TLC and QLC. BiCS8 introduced our CMOS Directly Bonded to Array, our CBA architecture, enabling the performance required by AI data center customers and establishing the framework for future generations.

Story Continues

BiCS9 pairs the proven BiCS8 cell array with next-generation CMOS, significantly increasing interface performance while retaining a mature memory architecture. BiCS10 advances the full node architecture across both TLC and QLC with a 1-terabit TLC die designed for performance-intensive workloads and a 2-terabit QLC die, delivering industry-leading density and twice the read and write bandwidth of BiCS8. Together, these technologies will extend the BiCS8 foundation to meet the evolving performance and capacity requirements of next-generation infrastructure. Beyond the core road map, High Bandwidth Flash, or HBF, reached an important milestone in the fiscal first quarter with the tape-out of our first HBF memory die with fabrication now underway.

As we outlined at Investor Day, HBF is a new memory architecture for inference that targets HBM class read bandwidth with substantially greater capacity to support larger models, longer context lengths and growing KV caches. It is designed to complement HBM by bringing NAND class capacity closer to the processor, and we remain on track to deliver samples of our first HBF-based products next calendar year. HBF remains a future innovation and is not included in the long-term financial model we introduced at Investor Day. As customer adoption, product requirements and manufacturing readiness become more clearly defined, we expect to provide further perspective on the market opportunity.

Customers recognize the strength of our innovation and increasingly view Sandisk as an important partner in achieving their growth objectives. Through our NBMs, we continue to evolve customer relationships into long-term partnerships grounded in innovation, collaboration and shared commitment. Our most recent customer engagements with the world's leading AI companies indicate further upside in demand for our technology. Our market-leading technology, product portfolio and customer partnerships are the backbone of our strong financial position, which allows us to reinvest to maintain our technology leadership and expand supply through R&D-focused CapEx. Each of these strengths is reinforced by tailwinds from AI. The need for scalable memory and storage is expanding as inference workloads grow, making NAND increasingly integral to AI infrastructure.

During inference, each generated token must reference the context that precedes it, creating a growing KV cache that serves as the model's working memory. Longer prompts, more complex reasoning, multimodal inputs and persistent user context materially increase these storage requirements. HBM and DRAM support the highest performance tier, while flash provides the capacity required to retain broader context efficiently and avoid costly recomputation. We believe this is a secular dynamic that is expanding NAND's role across the AI stack. The memory hierarchy defines the role of each NAND architecture. TLC provides the lower latency, higher write performance and greater endurance required for active data sets, checkpointing and latency-sensitive KV cache workloads.

In our AI lab comparison we presented at Investor Day, systems utilizing SSD delivered approximately 3x the token throughput while using approximately 75% less energy than comparable systems relying on volatile memory alone. QLC further increases storage density for capacity-intensive applications such as data lakes, vector databases that power AI search and retrieval repositories. Between these layers, a growing persistent context tier establishes data to be retained and recalled rather than regenerated.

As inference costs decline, we expect the adoption and usage to expand, supporting our view that KV cache will represent approximately 1/3 of the AI data center flash market by the end of the decade and that the AI data center opportunity will approach the size of the NAND industry today. Turning to our end markets. In data center, our portfolio addresses the full range of AI infrastructure requirements from performance-intensive enterprise SSDs to high-capacity platforms. Demand remains strong and continues to grow, and we estimate that data center has expanded from approximately 20% of industry bits early in the decade to roughly half of the industry bits today.

This structural shift in customer mix is reshaping industry economics and is central to the transformation underway at Sandisk. This quarter, data center again delivered strong growth and continued to outpace the broader market as we allocated more supply to address the growing demand from this end market. Edge is a large and strategically important market for Sandisk, spanning smartphones, PCs, automotive, tablets and an expanding range of physical AI applications. Automotive is becoming an increasingly important growth vector in our Edge business and a meaningful long-term growth opportunity. We have deepening engagements with leading customers, reinforcing our confidence that automotive can become one of the largest markets within Edge over time.

Our Consumer business remains a differentiated strategic asset, combining direct brand engagement with hundreds of millions of end users and broad shelf presence across the world's leading channel partners. The consumer end market provides a durable foundation for our business, while its direct connection to the market informs product development and provides early insight into shifts in end-user demand. Taken together, these results reinforce the durability of the model we outlined at our Investor Day. We have established a strong level of profitability and cash generation, and our focus from here is consistent execution across the portfolio. With that, I'll turn the call over to Luis for a detailed update on our business and outlook.

Luis Visoso: Thank you, David. We're executing the strategies and plans that we outlined at Investor Day, and we're delivering attractive financial results. In the first quarter, we closed 2 NBMs. Because both deals closed before our fourth quarter earnings call, we announced these partnerships on that call. We're in active conversations with existing NBM customers that are evaluating extending existing agreements and with new customers that are evaluating new NBMs. These long-term partnerships provide greater visibility into demand and financial performance, supporting a more durable financial model. We will remain patient and disciplined in selecting the right long-term partners as we define the optimal percentage of our bits that we allocate to NBMs, which is likely higher than our current levels.

Revenue for the first quarter was $11 billion, up 23% sequentially and 378% year-over-year. This compares favorably with our guidance range of $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion. Both volume growth and higher pricing contributed to revenue growth, with approximately 60% of the increase attributable to volume growth and 40% to higher pricing. Data center revenue was $4.8 billion, up 61% sequentially, outpacing estimated market growth for the quarter. Our leading products and strong customer partnerships, including 3 U.S. hyperscalers, underpin our continued expansion in this fast-growing end market. Edge revenue was $5.8 billion, up 7% sequentially, reflecting resilience in premium and mainstream markets, partially offset by contraction at the lower end.

Within Edge, we saw strong growth with automotive and IoT customers. Consumer revenue was $397 million, down 29% sequentially as the market adjusts to higher pricing. We remain committed to serving all 3 end markets with a diversified portfolio that optimizes our performance over time. Non-GAAP gross margin for the first quarter was 85.1%, up from 84.6% in the prior quarter, driven by higher volumes and pricing. This compares favorably with our guidance range of 83% to 85%. Non-GAAP operating expenses were $513 million, representing 4.7% of revenue. Non-GAAP operating margin was 80.4% compared to 79.2% in the prior quarter.

Non-GAAP EPS was $49.51, up from $39.25 in the prior quarter and $1.22 in the same quarter of the prior fiscal year. This compares favorably with our guidance range of $44 to $46. We closed the quarter with 154 million diluted shares outstanding. Key GAAP to non-GAAP reconciliation includes $91 million in stock-based compensation, representing 0.8% of revenue and $513 million gain on equity securities, primarily attributable to our investment in Nanya. During the quarter, we repurchased approximately 3.2 million shares of our common stock for $5 billion. Over the past 2 quarters, we have repurchased 6 million shares, representing approximately 4% of our total shares outstanding.

Our repurchases reflect our conviction in the long-term value of the business and our disciplined approach to capital allocation. We continue to invest appropriately in the business while returning 100% of excess cash to shareholders. Moving on to free cash flow. Cash flow from operations was $6.4 billion. Gross capital expenditures totaled $378 million, representing 3.4% of revenue. We expect gross capital spending to increase during the balance of the year and represent mid-single-digit percentage of revenue for fiscal year 2027. During the quarter, we generated $5.7 billion in adjusted free cash flow, representing approximately 52% margin. We closed the quarter with $5.1 billion in cash and cash equivalents and no debt. Moving on to guidance.

Our confidence in the long-term health of the market is reinforced by the structural growth of the AI infrastructure and the expanding role of NAND across inference workloads. Before turning to our second quarter outlook, I will announce that the Sandisk Board of Directors has approved an 8-for-1 stock split of the company's common stock. The additional shares are expected to be distributed on November 19 and trading on a split-adjusted basis is expected to begin on November 20. For the second quarter of fiscal year 2027, we expect revenue between $12.2 billion and $12.6 billion. We expect non-GAAP gross margin between 84.5% and 85.5%, which includes modest like-for-like price increases.

On a pre-split basis, we expect non-GAAP EPS between $55 and $57, assuming 151 million fully diluted shares. On an 8-for-1 split-adjusted basis, this equates to non-GAAP EPS between $6.88 and $7.13, assuming approximately 1,208 million fully diluted shares. For context, we expect a strong market in calendar year 2027. Data center is expected to be, again, the engine of growth and represent over 55% of the market with bit demand growing about 40% year-on-year, enabled by higher AI-driven capital spending. This is after more than doubling in 2026. Our NBM pipeline exceeds our supply throughout the end of the decade. With that, let me turn the call back to David.

David V. Goeckeler: Thank you, Luis. We continue to execute on the strategy we outlined at Investor Day, reinforcing our confidence in Sandisk's long-term trajectory. Our technology leadership, deep customer partnership and disciplined financial management, supported by a structural increase in NAND demand driven by AI, position us to serve our customers, deliver growing and durable free cash flow and return capital to shareholders. Over the past year, we have transformed the earnings and cash generation power of the business and established a strong foundation for durable performance. We remain focused on disciplined execution, sustained value creation and delivering against our long-term financial objectives. With that, Ivan, let's open it up for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question today comes from Ben Reitzes from Melius.

Benjamin Reitzes: I wanted to ask 2, if I could. One on the NBMs. You signed 2 before the last call. So I'm just wondering if we're going to have a lot more of them because it seems like you're already capacity constrained to agree to them. And then do you mind reminding us what the bits under contract will be in the next few years, if that's changed at all? And then I have a quick follow-up.

David V. Goeckeler: I'll make a few comments -- Thanks, Ben. We appreciate it. Always good to hear from you. So I'll make a few comments on NBMs, and then Luis will fill in. We've got a very strong pipeline of NBMs, and you kind of hit on all the issues there. As the portfolio gets more subscribed and more committed and we're at half the bits for this fiscal year and 2/3 for next year, it's a fitting exercise to get the next tranche of them in there. But the pipeline is very strong. I think we said last quarter -- I know we said last quarter that we're going to be patient and consider the next set of customers.

And that's exactly what we're doing. And we expect more of them over the next several months, several quarters as we continue to allocate the rest of the portfolio. So the pipeline is very strong and growing, quite frankly, and it's become the predominant way we deal with our customers. And I expect that the percent of the portfolio committed to continue to go up over the next couple of quarters. Luis?

Luis Visoso: Yes. I mean just a few things because I think David covered most of it. We feel very good about where we are with the NBMs. As you know, we've been very selective, very strategic in who we chose to sign these deals with. We're looking at the companies we have, and 95% of our NBMs are with companies that are investment grade, and they generated about $130 billion in operating cash flow. So we feel that we've made the right choices. And as David just mentioned, we'll continue to be patient. We'll continue to be selective, and the pipeline is terrific. So you should expect us to make -- continue to make progress.

I think in my prepared remarks, I said that we expect the bits to continue to grow. We had shared with you that about 50% of our bits are under NBM for '27 and about 2/3 for '28. And we expect that number to continue to go a little bit higher from the 2/3.

David V. Goeckeler: Ben, I'll just make one more comment. You got to ask 2 questions, so I'll make 2 comments. We're also balancing customers that are coming back for more, like that is a real thing. And in general, we're hearing from our customers that they have underestimated the amount of NAND they need to run their infrastructure. And so we have multiple customers coming back for a second round and then balancing that against bringing new customers into the portfolio. So there's a lot to sort out, and these are big, complicated agreements, but we feel very, very good about where the pipeline is, where the portfolio is at, the products are resonating.

And we'll continue to update you as we build out the portfolio of NBMs over the next couple of quarters.

Benjamin Reitzes: Okay. Great. And just a quick follow-up. You may have seen that Intel guided down for the next quarter due to PCs, and it really -- the impact of the memory is more than anybody thought, at least with their guidance. I don't know about anybody else. Just wondering if you are seeing NBM interest from those in the PC market more? And how you -- if there's -- if that market, with regard to some of the device makers, is something that will become an NBM or is actually now getting more attractive because they're willing to pay more? How should we think about that as it looks like they're starved for product and missing numbers in that segment?

Luis Visoso: I mean, Ben, we have -- we cannot talk about specific customers. What we've said in the past is we do have NBMs in the data center business. It's data center-centric, but we also have customers on the edge. And we've offered this construct to any customer that wants it and start a process where it makes sense. So we're not trying to restrict it from any customer. We're open for business.

David V. Goeckeler: So Ben, the other thing I'll say to this. I mean, we are looking at this in our own reviews. We know that units were down this year. They're going to be slightly down next year, low single digits. I mean these 2 calendar quarters right now are really the trough of the year-over-year compares where they're the most negative. And so this is where we're feeling the biggest amount of change in that market on a unit basis, on a year-over-year basis. All that said, we expect the PC exabytes to grow next year.

And in fact, we think our internal models are every segment in the NAND market, PCs, smartphones, data center will all show positive growth next year because of content per device continues to go up as part of that is mixing to premium. So there's no doubt there's been a market adjustment. In many ways, we're in the -- as I said, from a unit basis, we're in the teeth of that on a year-over-year basis, but we see improvement from here.

Operator: Our next question comes from Joe Moore from Morgan Stanley.

Joseph Moore: It seems like the underlying story here, in addition to just how good the market is, is your presence in data center. You're up almost 20x year-on-year, up 61% sequentially. Can you talk about -- obviously, the market is good, but it seems like your participation is also a lot better. Is that because of BiCS8? Is that just because the market is different? Just what is it that's allowing you to get to those levels of penetration? And if data center is half of bits at some point, will you get to that in your own mix as well?

David V. Goeckeler: Yes, Joe, so thanks for the comment. We feel very good about where we're at in data center. I mean anything where you see the kind of numbers we posted year-over-year is a combination of things. I mean it starts with the fundamental NAND node. BiCS8 is a very good node. CBA gives you very, very clean CMOS, which is very good interface speeds, all those kinds of things. We built the right products. We've had a TLC product in the market for several years now. It was just a couple of quarters ago that we started selling our QLC product for revenue and that -- we expected that to ramp, and that's happening.

So we got the right product at the right time based on the right technology. And then over the last quarter or so, there's been a lot more refinement of the AI inference architecture is what I would say. When I look at the market and we kind of decompose it internally, customers are just getting more refined about how they're using NAND, where they're using TLC, where they're using QLC, all different phases from KV cache to staging, to fast data lakes and all the subparts of those markets, inference and agent orchestration, model pre-training, model post-training. There's just a general -- we're seeing NAND be applied in a more, I would say, nuanced way.

In the past, QLC is being used in the right places. And you're even seeing QLC, some customers even move into like KV cache where they can be supported. On the other side of the spectrum, we're seeing SLC being pulled into the architecture. It's not really in sales yet. It's more in architectural conversations. And it's not a performance type of conversation. It's more endurance, during agentic workloads, the amount of endurance required. And in that place, it's kind of where can we substitute NAND for DRAM. And we think those kind of architectures will be very sticky over time. Once you make that transition, you're going to stick with it given the price differential.

So we see all of these things working together. And I think these NBMs set us up for these very deep and strategic level conversations with our customers about how they're using our product, deep discussions with our engineers about how they could use our product to solve different use cases. And all of that is leading to a tremendous pull on our portfolio. And like I said, our biggest customers, we've already signed one second tranche of an NBM, and we're in discussions in others. So the whole setup is very strong, and we feel good about it, and we appreciate your recognition of the performance on a year-over-year basis. It really is quite outstanding.

Joseph Moore: It is surprising. And where do you think the mix goes long term in terms of good over half...

David V. Goeckeler: So we're working hard to catch up to have our portfolio mix equal what the market bits are. And we're going to continue to make progress throughout calendar year '27. We'll see if we actually catch up by the end of the quarter, but I think we'll get to a substantially higher number on mix than we are if we look back at calendar year -- or fiscal year '26. We'll continue to make progress here.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mark Newman from Bernstein.

Mark Newman: On the -- if I could just, first of all, talk about price and volume in the guidance. You talked about in the fiscal Q1 that you just reported, I think you said 60% of the revenue growth from volume and 40% from pricing. Baked into your guide, I mean, how do you expect that mix to progress? Any comments on pricing? I appreciate that you've got a very high portion of the volumes on these NBMs, but still wanted to get some clarity on pricing. I think there's a comment that modest improvement in pricing in FQ2. Any further clarity on that?

And then I have a follow-on question on HBF and some of the new NAND technologies as well.

Luis Visoso: So let me take the first one. Yes, you're right. We reported 60% -- about 60% of the revenue growth came from volume and 40% from pricing in Q1 roughly. And we do expect both to contribute in the next quarter. We normally don't break this, Mark, into its pieces, but we do expect some modest pricing as we put in our prepared remarks. So we do expect both to contribute during the quarter, and we expect pricing to continue to increase modestly throughout the year.

Mark Newman: That's helpful. Fair enough. And follow-up question is on HBF and other new NAND technologies in the data center. So there was a comment about some progress on HBF, which was great to hear. But I wondered if there's any more comments on progress and discussions with partners and customers, anything there? And the other thing, Dave, you mentioned about some of the other new NAND technologies in the data center, Storage-Next, and then there's also the CMX context memory. Just what's your view on all these types of new NAND tiers in the data center? Do you think that they all win?

Just any kind of comments on the interplay of all these and the roles for each and how SanDisk plays in them and the timing would be really appreciated.

David V. Goeckeler: Sure. So Mark, the conversations with potential customers on HBF are robust and continue to be -- we'll continue to have those conversations as we go into putting product samples in their hands so they can start to use and understand how it's going to fit in their system. So we'll continue to update on that, but it's kind of an always-on conversation. Your second question, I think this is like very, very healthy for where AI inference is, which is as it scales out, it needs to be -- the architecture is just being relentlessly refined for economics.

And that's a very good thing because it's going to -- if it's going to scale, the more economic it is, the better. And that's pulling NAND into more parts of the architecture because NAND is the most scalable semiconductor technology, right? So we're seeing -- like I said, we're seeing -- if you would go back a couple of years ago, it was all about going for more density again, going from TLC to QLC. We're still doing that, right? That's still a big part of the strategy. But now, there's some of it even going in the other direction. How do I use -- how do I get more endurance in specific parts of the architecture?

Is the endurance and the performance I get out of NAND good enough to solve the use case at a part of the architecture where I can use it over competing technologies that may be significantly more expensive and difficult to acquire. So I would say this is a very, very dynamic discussion. There's a lot of ideas on the table. I think there should be a lot of ideas on the table. I think they'll all be pursued.

And I think that it is -- the most important thing is to stay close to the people that are spending the money to scale the infrastructure because in the end, they'll make the decisions of what's right for them based on the use cases they're trying to solve at scale and where they're putting all this money behind it. And we're deeply engaged in those conversations, and I expect them to continue to be very robust and have a lot of different ideas about how we could stretch our technology in different directions to fit more and more use cases. And building a product, it's always the same thing.

I want the right technology at the right time and the right intensity at the right cost and really not anything less or anything more. And that's what building a product is all about because you can deliver it at the right price and then you can get the right return on it. So that process is full on in AI inference architecture working with our customers.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Gibson from MST Financial.

David Gibson: A really great quarter. Well done. Can you hear me?

David V. Goeckeler: Yes, yes. Hi, David.

David Gibson: Just a quick one. Just wondering whether you're looking to accelerate the BiCS transition from 8 to 9, 10 and so forth as a way to accelerate the bit growth in the short term and satisfy some of that very strong customer demand?

David V. Goeckeler: No. I mean we're committed to the bit growth we talked about, mid- to high teens. Those nodal transitions require a lot of planning and tool purchases and where lines are set up. So we're still -- we have that fab plan set up for the kind of bit growth we've been talking about for a long time. So no plans to change that at this point.

David Gibson: Okay. And just one follow-up. You talked about earlier about allocating more supply to the data center in Q1. Are there any limits to increasingly allocating your bits to data center?

David V. Goeckeler: Well, I mean, it's very -- in some ways, yes. I mean, out of the fab, you come out with a certain mix of TLC, QLC, certain die mix, all these kinds of issues. So it's a constant fitting exercise of getting the right product to the right customer. And there's a lot of magic that goes on in the organization, and Luis's organization is a big part of that, working with our sales teams of what is the available inventory, what's coming out of the fab, what's the mix, and where is it all going to go. Do you want to say a little bit more about that, Luis?

Luis Visoso: Yes. I think the only thing I would add, obviously, it changes depending on the time frame you're looking at. Over the short term, it's almost impossible to do anything. It takes 120 days or so to produce a wafer. But obviously, as you look further out, there are more degrees of freedom.

Operator: Our next question comes from C.J. Muse from Cantor Fitzgerald.

Christopher Muse: Just a question on the comment around your NBM pipeline exceeding supply through the end of the decade in the slide deck. I guess, can you elaborate on that? And how is that changing kind of your thought process around what bit supply will look like for the industry over the next handful of years? And how are you adjusting, if at all, your CapEx plans? I know you talked about mid-single digits, which implies roughly $2.5 billion to $3 billion gross CapEx, fairly low kind of number. So I would love to hear kind of your thoughts on how the visibility is impacting your thoughts around bit growth and supply.

David V. Goeckeler: Well, I mean, I think my -- first thing I'd say about it, C.J., is the process is working. I mean it was only 2 or 3 quarters ago, we talked about even instituting this kind of business model. And we had some customers that were like-minded, and we made some very good progress. And here we are a couple of quarters later, and it's -- we talked about this after our Investor Day, we had customers coming to us offering NBMs. And that now becomes -- it's not the only way we do business. There's lots of customers with lots of different volume levels and different products, and we want to meet our customers where they are.

There's no doubt about that. But it's very good to see that we have a robust pipeline now through the end -- through 2030, and we're even getting beyond that, as we talked about, of customers that are really willing to give us their demand signals and financial commitments. And to the question earlier, those kinds of things will allow us, if we choose to, to eventually start changing supply and demand and all those kinds of things. But we're just not there yet, right? We got to go through negotiations on all of those. We've got to get commitments. We've got to get everything all aligned.

But I would say that the process is working well, and we're very happy with where it's at, and it gives us a lot more visibility into how we plan. But the process is still underway, right? It's still underway. And we'll -- as I said, we'll continue to update you over the next couple of quarters as we make progress.

Christopher Muse: Just a quick follow-up for Luis. On these contracts and considering some have deposits, are you able to use those deposits for buybacks? Or is that cash restricted?

Luis Visoso: Yes. In theory, we could, C.J. But as we explained at Analyst Day, the vast majority are financial guarantees, which are held by third-party financial institutions. So they are not in my balance sheet. The only thing that's in the balance sheet is prepayments, and we -- that's, by far, the smallest amount. But there is no legal restriction on that.

Operator: Our next question comes from Karl Ackerman from BNP Paribas.

Karl Ackerman: It's encouraging to see increasing NAND content for xPU and AI servers to support KV cache demand, which, I think, compares to reductions in memory content in some server SKUs. But Dave, could you discuss how you see enterprise SSD content per server progressing in 2027 in the context of this agentic AI proliferation? Because it's certainly becoming a larger portion of your portfolio.

David V. Goeckeler: That's a big question, Karl. I mean, look, what we're doing is there's no doubt in inference and agent orchestration that our product is tied to kind of CPU demand in -- for those type of applications. I mean we know at a pretty granular level the amount of demand that we expect per CPU, something 60 to 90 gigabytes per CPU is what we see in those kind of applications. I haven't run the math against what the server TAM is and kind of what the elasticity is between those 2, but we can follow up on that.

But as I said earlier, we continue to see more NAND being pulled into the inference architecture in all parts of the architecture and in very different ways, right? TLC, QLC and as I said earlier, now, people looking for high endurance solutions that will fit parts of the workload where they don't need to use DRAM and they can use that type of NAND. So it's all very encouraging, and we'll continue to stay close. But we'll do some work on the 2 TAM analysis and what the trade-offs are between them.

Karl Ackerman: Sure. If I may, a quick follow-up. Do you have an updated view or progress on your goal for enterprise SSD share? I mean, can you achieve perhaps that low to mid-teens share in 2027 because you're seeing quite success right now?

David V. Goeckeler: We've tried not -- I mean, in the past, like many, many years ago, we put some share goals out there, and I've tried very hard not to put share goals out there because sometimes it leads to kind of perverse choices in the portfolio. We want to maximize the value of the portfolio across all time horizons, near term, midterm, long term. So we want to keep some balance into it. Clearly, we're going to mix higher into data center. I mean you see that. We talked about that earlier. I think 17x growth year-over-year. You don't see a 17x very often in a business at this scale.

And as I said, I expect that to go higher as we go through '27. And the balance point, in some ways, will be dependent -- will depend quarter-by-quarter what we see and then what NBMs we sign, right? Those will give us a big -- a lot of visibility over the next several years where we see that mix going. So it's going higher, but I'm not going to put a specific target out there.

Operator: Our next question comes from Vijay Rakesh from Mizuho.

Vijay Rakesh: Great quarter and guide. Just a quick question. As you look at data center, 2027 looks like, you mentioned, 40% demand bit growth, which is massive. As you look at this BiCS8, BiCS9, BiCS10 transition, do they help you drive some bits to meet that demand? How is the supply on that side, I guess? I have a quick follow-up.

David V. Goeckeler: Look, I mean, BiCS8, BiCS9, BiCS9 is a big part of a data center strategy of being able to get faster interface speeds with the same cell and kind of what CBA gives us that flexibility we talked about at Investor Day. So in that sense, yes, those are big parts of the strategy. There's no doubt about it. So as I said earlier, it's about getting the right product to the right customer. And the TLC product has been performing very, very well for quite some time now. And now we're seeing the ramping of QLC. And we'll see some ramp of BiCS9, but BiCS10 is still a little ways out, right?

I mean we announced BiCS10, but we're still ramping BiCS8. So we've got a ways to go before we get out to some of those future BiCS nodes.

Vijay Rakesh: Got it. And then on the endurance side, as you mentioned, some of your peers talking about SLC NAND out there. Any thoughts how that plays out next year? Obviously, that could tighten up the NAND market as well in addition to what you're seeing in just overall demand growth, I guess.

David V. Goeckeler: Yes, I think it's a little early to have a very strong view on that, right? We are talking to some customers that are giving us some signals of demand for SLC. I mean, clearly, you start mixing SLC and you're going to take away -- there's a clear trade ratio of 3:1, 4:1, whether it's TLC or QLC. So it will impact the overall supply in the market depending on how much SLC is used and how much really gets deployed. But it's a little early to put a specific forecast on it right now.

What I would say, it's an architectural discussion and a request from customers of better understanding the technology and how it could fit parts of the use case as they build out their inference architecture. So we'll update you as we go over the next couple of quarters, and we'll see how this develops, but definitely something to keep an eye on.

Operator: Our next question comes from Jim Schneider from Goldman Sachs.

James Schneider: I was wondering maybe on a more tactical basis, your consumer business obviously has seasonality in Q1 historically. And obviously, the PC business does too, but data center is in sort of secular growth mode. So Luis, based on your visibility at this point, I'm just wondering if you could maybe give us any kind of color on whether you'd expect Q1 to be sequentially up, down or sideways, roughly?

Luis Visoso: So fiscal Q3, you mean?

James Schneider: Yes, fiscal, the March quarter.

Luis Visoso: So if you look at historically, right, our Q3 is normally our weakest sequential quarter. So last quarter, for example, our bits were down 19% sequentially. So if I -- we're not guiding Q3. But for modeling purposes, I would be conservative in your sequential growth from Q2 to Q3.

James Schneider: And then just as a matter of principle on the buyback, good to see the continued execution there. I'm sort of curious, as you sort of start to run down the authorization, would you expect the Board to re-up their authorization on a quarterly basis? Or maybe you could provide us any more color on how you're thinking about executing on the actual buybacks given a much lower stock price today?

David V. Goeckeler: So we're -- we have a very clear strategy. 100% of excess cash is going to go back to shareholders. We're going to execute that aggressively or appropriately. And we know how to get a hold of the Board. We have meetings every quarter. And so I don't expect any impedance on that side of the -- from us about how we execute. I expect us to continue to be -- I don't expect us to be, we will be, continue to be faithful to our strategy, which is we're going to return 100% of excess cash to shareholders. We're off to a good start, I think, over the last couple of quarters.

I think we bought back 4% of the market cap of the shares outstanding of where we started, and we're going to continue to execute that program appropriately.

Operator: And our next question comes from Krish Sankar from TD Cowen.

Kinney Chin: This is Steven calling on behalf of Krish. First question I have for Dave. I guess looking at your CSP customer base, I kind of wanted to get some color on what the prevailing demand currently is between TLC versus QLC bits? And kind of going forward with the NBMs in place, does that TLC versus QLC mix shift meaningfully later this decade?

David V. Goeckeler: We're still like at that 70-30 number on TLC to QLC. TLC has been a big driver of the portfolio. We are hearing more from our customers about a reacceleration of QLC in different use cases. And so we'll see how that plays out, as you said, through the end of the decade. But that's where it is. I mean, that 70-30 number is a pretty good number. And of course, there's some fluctuation quarter-to-quarter, a little bit up and down here and there, but that's where it's been, and that's where we expect it to be, at least for the next -- the rest of this fiscal year.

Let me put that time horizon on it, and then we'll see where -- what customers are thinking about QLC as we continue to have those discussions. And I will say the ramp -- the Stargate product has been -- which is our QLC product. There's too many internal names here, but it's been very well received. It was not that many quarters ago that we were talking about going through qualifications. That's all 100% behind us. Customers are ramping. It's been a very, very well-received product and a very key part of the portfolio.

Kinney Chin: Got you. And as a quick follow-up, a question on the mobile edge market. Just given the double-digit unit declines in that market this year as well, but albeit concentrated in the kind of entry and mid-tier of the market. I'm kind of curious like from the demand signals that some of your customers in that market are giving you, can your mobile bits still grow next year overall?

David V. Goeckeler: Yes. I think -- let's talk about the market first. I mean -- you got it. I mean the low end is under pressure, but that leads to a unit decline, but a content per unit increasing. So when you add it all up, we expect growth of exabytes in that market next year on a slightly declining unit count. As far as our portfolio, I mean, we don't -- it's kind of like data center. I don't want to make projections on individual markets. We will manage the portfolio with agility and flexibility.

We've been very clear that we want balance in the portfolio, but we're going to optimize the financial outcome over the short, mid and long term, kind of integrate those to get the best outcome. And we'll update you on what the mix of mobile is as we go forward.

Operator: Our next question comes from Wamsi Mohan from Bank of America.

Wamsi Mohan: In your slide deck, you say leading AI companies could indicate further demand upside. I was wondering if these are AI labs or neoclouds? And are any of the credit concerns around the neoclouds filtering back to you in any way that you can see at the moment? And I have a follow-up.

Luis Visoso: We haven't seen any of that. To the contrary, we're seeing very strong demand from our customers. And as I said, if I look at our largest customers, they're basically all investment-grade companies, right, generating very strong cash. So we're not seeing any impacts from any credit issues whatsoever if they are out in the market. And demand from our customers is, if anything, strengthening versus what it was a quarter ago.

Wamsi Mohan: So to clarify there, Luis, when you say leading AI companies, are you referring to AI labs over there?

Luis Visoso: We sell to everybody in our business. We sell to hyperscalers. We sell to model makers. We sell to everybody.

Wamsi Mohan: Okay. And then just on linearity in the quarter. It seems like receivables picked up a little bit. Is that something that we should expect because of payment terms as more bits go under NBM? Or was there something else in the quarter?

Luis Visoso: No. We basically saw a little bit of a change in customer mix, and that has a little bit of an impact on our receivables, a little bit on linearity, but it's mostly customer mix.

Operator: Our next question comes from Amit Daryani from Evercore.

Amit Daryanani: I guess, David, just to start with on the capital allocation side, as you transition towards becoming a more predictable NBM-driven business model, does that change how you think about your capital structure? And historically, I think memory is perceived to be more cyclical, so balance sheet flexibility has been important. But as you become structurally, I think, less cyclical, would that support a willingness to take on leverage and potentially accelerate the capital returns? Or is the comfort still with the $5 billion a quarter buyback, which is fairly impressive? I'm just wondering, at what point do you say we can take on more leverage and take advantage of the fact that we're less cyclical?

David V. Goeckeler: I mean we put a financial model out. I mean we just talked -- we just spent 3.5 hours talking about this in our Analyst Day, and we committed to a financial model through the end of the -- through 2030, which I think was pretty impressive. And we plan to execute that, and we're very comfortable with the strategy we have of staying debt-free, very strong balance sheet and then returning -- investing in our business. We have a growing business and lots of opportunities for internal innovation, which we're going to continue to invest in like HBF and 3D Matrix Memory in addition to the BiCS road map and all the great products we build.

And after we do that, we're going to return 100% of the cash flow to shareholders. And that's the plan, and we're going to go execute that for the foreseeable future until we get up at another point and tell you we're going to change it. But I don't anticipate that happening in any kind of near-term time frame.

Amit Daryanani: Fair enough. And then maybe just on HBF and rather than trying to ask you to frame how big this TAM could be. Could you just talk about what the scaling variable really is over here as inference models and context windows expand? Should we think HBF capacity will grow in line to GPU compute or potentially faster? And I think you said you'll start initial sampling in '27. What are the key milestones from there to becoming a meaningful revenue ramp as well?

David V. Goeckeler: Well, I mean -- so it's a little early for your first question. But on the second question, we get the die back. We have the base die, which we'll tape out, which is the controller, we'll put them together, put it in customers' hands. And then they start to see how the product is going to work in their infrastructure.

We've obviously done a lot of modeling on that, but actually having the actual product and then doing the integration work, that will then lead -- that kind of feedback from the customer will then lead to be able to start to answer some of the questions that people have, like what's the market opportunity, how fast is it going to happen, what's the TAM, where exactly is the architecture going to fit. We're going to follow our customers on that.

But the big step is to actually put a product in their hands, and then that leads to a whole another set of conversations with them where we actually have the device that we're -- instead of running simulations, we're seeing exactly how it performs in their infrastructure and does it deliver the results of what they're expecting. And we'll also -- that also helps you continue to expand the set of use cases, right? At this point in the development process, you want to be a little bit careful. You don't engage too much because you're overwhelming your engineering team with 1,000 ideas of how the product can be used.

So as we get actual device that we can put in people's hands, we can open the aperture on those kind of conversations, which will -- I think will lead to more use cases for the product. But that's still TBD. So I think a lot of things start to happen when you get to that next milestone of actually having a real product that people can start to -- they can start to use and understand how it impacts what they're trying to do, which is deliver a world-class inference architecture at the best cost point possible. And we think this is a fantastic technology for doing that, but we'll see when we get there and we produce it.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mehdi Hosseini from SIG.

Mehdi Hosseini: David, I want to go back to -- sorry for the audio. David, I want to go back to what you said earlier. You said that AI inferencing is being refined, having an impact and more SLC needed. And my question to you is, is this having an adverse impact on adoption of TLC or the growth of TLC, or SLC is additive to the bit demand by TLC and QLC?

David V. Goeckeler: No, I don't think it's a cannibalization of other NAND products. I think it's an expansion of the TAM into areas that you need different attributes of the technology. You need different endurance, you need different performance. And we can take our product and we can run anything out of the fab in an SLC mode. So there's a lot of flexibility in the product. And I think our people are discovering that and starting to understand how can I apply this in ways where I get the attributes I want for the problem I'm trying to solve.

So it's just a more refined view of the architecture, but I don't see it as cannibalizing other parts of the NAND stack. If anything, I see it as -- and I want to be careful on this because it's still early, but it's -- is it good enough to replace places where I'm using DRAM, right? Can I get enough endurance? Can I get enough performance if I run NAND in an SLC mode? Because the cost differential is like huge, 20 to 40x. So I take it as a very healthy sign on many ways, Mehdi. One is that very, very real about how you scale an architecture.

When you scale an architecture, you got to do it in the most cost-effective way possible. And again, NAND is the most scalable semiconductor technology. And so it doesn't surprise me that people are finding more ways to use it. In many ways, I think scalable technologies kind of attract TAM. And I think that's what's happening here as these architectures are getting more detailed and more refined.

Mehdi Hosseini: Okay. Let me come at it from a different angle. And if there is this demand for more enduring SLC and as customers wait for commercialization of HBF, what is the JV's flexibility in adding some SLC capacity to meet that short-term demand?

David V. Goeckeler: No, we don't -- I mean, we don't -- there is no -- I mean, I wouldn't think of it as SLC capacity. You can take any -- our cells are flexible enough that we can run them in whatever mode we want, SLC, MLC, TLC. So we can supply the market with the wafers we have, right? That's how we think about it. And I understand the question of wanting to go to the supply question right away, but it's just like super early for that. These are just conversations at this point and customers exploring how they can use the technology, starting to get some idea of what their demand would be if they use it this way.

It's something to keep your eye on. It will impact the market, no doubt about that, because SLC is -- a little bit of SLC is a lot of QLC. But I guess more to come, Mehdi.

Operator: And at this point, ladies and gentlemen, we'll be ending today's question-and-answer session. I'd like to turn the floor back over to management for any closing remarks.

David V. Goeckeler: All right, everyone. Thanks for joining us on the call. We appreciate it. Great conversation, and we look forward to seeing you throughout the quarter. Thank you.

Luis Visoso: Thank you.

Operator: And with that, we'll conclude today's conference call and presentation. We do thank you for joining. You may now disconnect your lines.

news.Title: Sandisk: Why The Panic Over A NAND Slowdown May Be Overdone
news.Content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

Sandisk ( NASDAQ:SNDK ) shares have slid to about $1,400 from the $1,800 range reached in late September, even as the outlook for NAND flash memory may remain supportive.

NAND is a type of memory used to store data in devices such as solid-state drives, or SSDs. Demand tied to artificial intelligence has absorbed much of the available supply.

Some investors have grown cautious. GF Securities has said NAND price gains could slow to low single digits in the fourth quarter, and China-based YMTC has claimed technology breakthroughs that raise fears of a flood of supply.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 3 Warning Signs with SNDK.

Is SNDK fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The firm argues pricing remains firm. TrendForce projects fourth-quarter enterprise SSD contract prices to rise 23% to 28% from the prior quarter, while overall NAND prices are seen up 15% to 20%. Consumer demand is weakening as buyers resist higher prices.

Sandisk estimates data centers account for 50% of flash bits shipped today, up from 30% last year. It also says NAND capacity remains about 30% below the 2022 peak.

Micron (MU) CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said he expects memory supply and demand conditions to be tighter in 2027 and 2028 than in 2026. He sees NAND staying supply constrained in both years.

Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix are putting DRAM and high-bandwidth memory ahead of NAND in capital spending, which may keep NAND prices elevated.

It expects AI spending to reach $1 trillion or more in 2027.

news.Title: MRVL vs. SNDK: Which AI Infrastructure Stock is a Safer Bet?
news.Content:
Marvell Technology MRVL and Sandisk SNDK are benefiting from the expanding artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure market, but their businesses address different requirements. Marvell develops custom silicon, networking and connectivity solutions that help AI systems process and transmit data. Sandisk supplies NAND flash-based storage products, including enterprise solid-state drives (SSDs), that support data-intensive workloads.

As AI infrastructure spending expands, both companies have opportunities to grow revenues and earnings. However, differences in growth visibility, profitability, valuation and execution risks raise the question: Which stock is the better investment right now?

The Case for MRVL Stock

Marvell is benefiting from rising demand for custom AI silicon, high-speed optical interconnects and advanced networking solutions. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, revenues increased 36.5% year over year to $2.74 billion, while non-GAAP earnings rose 40.3% to 94 cents per share. Data center revenues reached a record $2.17 billion, up 46% year over year, accounting for 79% of total revenues.

The company is expanding its AI infrastructure portfolio as hyperscalers invest in larger and more complex AI clusters. Demand for 800G optical digital signal processors remains strong, while 1.6T products are ramping rapidly. Marvell also expects its scale-out switching business to more than double in fiscal 2027, supported by wider adoption of its 51.2T products.

Custom silicon represents another important growth opportunity. Management expects the business to more than double year over year in fiscal 2028, with further acceleration anticipated in fiscal 2029. Marvell's expanded commercial agreement with a key hyperscaler covers existing and potential programs involving AI accelerators, storage controllers, network interface cards and memory interface controllers.

Strategic ties with NVIDIA and the acquisitions of Celestial AI and XConn Technologies further expand Marvell's opportunities in optical interconnects and next-generation AI networking. Management expects fiscal 2027 revenues to increase approximately 45% to $12 billion and fiscal 2028 revenues to reach roughly $18 billion, implying growth of about 50% in the latter year.

Nevertheless, Marvell faces margin pressure as custom silicon scales, along with customer concentration, supply constraints, geopolitical exposure and uneven communications demand. Its growing dependence on data center customers makes execution and hyperscaler spending particularly important. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MRVL's fiscal 2027 earnings suggests year-over-year growth of 48%. Estimates have remained unchanged in the past 30 days.

Story Continues

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

The Case for SNDK Stock

Sandisk is benefiting from accelerating demand for enterprise storage as AI workloads require greater capacity and performance. The company's first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenues surged 378% year over year and increased 23% sequentially to $11.03 billion. SNDK's data center revenues increased 61% sequentially to $4.80 billion, reflecting strong demand for enterprise SSDs across hyperscalers and AI infrastructure customers.

The company reported significant growth in its TLC enterprise SSD business and continued ramping of its QLC products, which address capacity-intensive applications such as AI data lakes, vector databases and retrieval repositories. SNDK's edge revenues rose 7% sequentially to $5.83 billion, supported by resilience in premium and mainstream markets and stronger automotive and IoT demand.

Sandisk's technology roadmap, including BiCS8, BiCS9 and BiCS10, supports higher storage density, interface performance and bandwidth. BiCS9 is expected to improve interface performance through next-generation CMOS, while BiCS10 introduces a 1-terabit TLC die for performance-intensive workloads and a 2-terabit QLC die with twice the read and write bandwidth of BiCS8. Its high-bandwidth flash (HBF) technology also advanced during the quarter, with the first HBF memory die completing tape-out and fabrication underway.

Sandisk expects to deliver samples of its first HBF-based products in 2027, although this opportunity is not yet included in its long-term financial model. SNDK's profitability and cash generation remain strong. Sandisk's non-GAAP gross margin increased to 85.1% from 84.6% in the preceding quarter, while non-GAAP operating margin improved to 80.4% from 79.2%. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for SNDK's fiscal 2027 earnings suggests year-over-year growth of 200%. Estimates have been revised upward in the past seven days.

Stock Price Performance and Valuation of MRVL & SNDK

In the year-to-date period, MRVL shares have gained 157% compared with the surge of 460.4% in SNDK shares.

YTD Performance Chart

SNDK is trading at a forward sales multiple of 3.29X, way below its median of 4.11X. MRVL's forward sales multiple sits at 9.90X, higher than its median of 9.44X over the past year.

Forward 12-Month (P/S) Valuation Chart

Conclusion: MRVL vs. SNDK

Sandisk appears better positioned than Marvell at present, supported by significantly stronger revenue growth, expanding profitability and a more attractive valuation. While Marvell offers promising opportunities in custom AI silicon, optical interconnects and networking, Sandisk is benefiting from the growing importance of NAND storage in AI infrastructure, with data center revenues accelerating rapidly. This is strongly supported by SNDK's massive bottom-line growth projection. SNDK and MRVL carry a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy) each at present. You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here .

news.Title: FORM's HBM and Foundry Testing Gain From AI Demand: What's Ahead?
news.Content:
FormFactor Inc. FORM is benefiting from rising demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced semiconductor testing as artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure expands. Increasing test complexity across memory, data-center CPUs, GPUs and custom application-specific integrated circuits is supporting growth in its Probe Cards business.

Broader exposure to foundry and logic applications is also expanding the company's growth opportunities beyond memory. FormFactor's DRAM revenues reached $84.9 million in the third quarter of 2026, up 24.5% year over year from $68.2 million. The results indicate continued strength in advanced memory testing, although DRAM revenue growth moderated from the previous quarter's record level.

Demand for advanced memory testing remains an important growth driver as HBM and other memory technologies require increasingly sophisticated testing capabilities. However, FormFactor's third-quarter financial disclosures do not specify HBM's share of DRAM sales or provide an update on SmartMatrix adoption and HBM4 testing activity.

FormFactor's Foundry & Logic business continued to gain momentum, with revenues increasing 44.2% year over year to $134 million in the third quarter of 2026 compared with $92.9 million in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, revenues rose 10% from $121.8 million in the second quarter. Foundry & Logic remained the largest contributor to the Probe Cards segment, which generated $221.1 million in third-quarter revenues, up from $209.7 million in the preceding quarter.

These results highlight the growing contribution of advanced semiconductor testing to FormFactor's business, although the third-quarter supplemental financial information does not break out the specific end-market drivers of Foundry & Logic growth. The company's fourth-quarter 2026 outlook points to continued broad-based demand strength, with total revenues projected at $285 million.

How Competitors Fare Against FORM

FORM competes with Teradyne TER in automated test equipment and KLA Corporation KLAC in semiconductor inspection/process control and wafer fabrication. KLA remains positioned to outperform as AI infrastructure spending broadens demand for process control across leading-edge logic, memory and advanced packaging.

Rising chip complexity, larger die sizes and tighter defect requirements should increase inspection and metrology intensity. Teradyne is entering a multiyear growth phase as AI investment expands test needs across compute, memory, networking, storage, power and data center systems. Rising wafer capacity, transistor growth and advanced packaging are TER's major growth drivers.

Shares of FORM have surged 74.7% year to date compared with the Zacks Electronics - Semiconductors industry's growth of 22.4%.

news.Title: NVTS Gears Up to Report Q3 Earnings: Buy, Sell or Hold the Stock?
news.Content:

Navitas Semiconductor is a well-known provider of power semiconductors, driven by its gallium nitride (GaN) business, under GaNFast, GaNSafe and GaNSense brands, along with silicon carbide (SiC) devices. Navitas Semiconductor is expected to have benefited from the growing demand for power that is served by the company's GaN and SiC technologies.

As AI infrastructure spending continues to grow, Navitas Semiconductor remains well-positioned to benefit from higher demand for its GaN and SiC products. These are likely to have hurt the company's prospects in the near term.

news.Title: Twilio Q3 Earnings Beat Estimates on Strong Revenue Growth
news.Content:
Twilio Inc. TWLO reported better-than-expected third-quarter 2026 results, with both earnings and revenues surpassing the Zacks Consensus Estimate. Non-GAAP earnings of $1.65 per share beat the consensus mark by 13%. The bottom line increased 32% from the year-ago quarter's earnings of $1.25 per share, driven by robust revenue growth and operating leverage.

The cloud-based communications platform provider reported revenues of $1.56 billion, surpassing the consensus estimate by 3.1%. Revenues increased 20% year over year, driven by broad-based product strength and growing AI-related demand. The dollar-based net expansion rate was 114%, up from 109% a year ago.

TWLO's Q3 Revenue Growth Drivers

Twilio's organic revenues increased 16% year over year to $1.50 billion. Organic growth excludes incremental U.S. carrier pass-through fees and acquisition-related revenues. The company benefited from healthy demand across messaging, voice and software add-ons, alongside sustained momentum among AI-native customers.

Messaging revenues grew 24% year over year, supported by higher volumes and increased adoption of WhatsApp and Rich Communication Services. Incremental U.S. carrier fees contributed approximately seven percentage points to messaging revenue growth. Messaging accounted for 59% of total revenues during the quarter.

Voice revenues increased more than 20%, reflecting higher usage volumes and growing adoption of software add-ons. The self-serve channel registered revenue growth exceeding 30%, while independent software vendor revenues advanced more than 20%. Software add-on revenues grew more than 25%, and support and services revenues increased more than 30%.

Twilio's AI Momentum Supports Customer Expansion

Twilio witnessed continued adoption of its AI-enabled communications capabilities, including Conversation Relay, Conversational Intelligence and Branded Calling. Management highlighted growing demand from AI-native businesses deploying voice agents and expanding their usage across multiple communication channels.

The company secured several notable customer agreements during the quarter. Ushur signed a seven-figure expansion involving voice AI capabilities, while Gong renewed a seven-figure agreement. Twilio also secured its first eight-figure Conversations deal with a health insurance provider, underscoring growing enterprise interest in AI-powered customer engagement.

Story Continues

Management noted that voice AI represents approximately 1% of overall voice interactions, highlighting the early stage of adoption. Twilio is also developing identity verification capabilities for AI agents, with an offering currently in private beta and general availability planned for 2027.

TWLO's Profitability Improves Despite Carrier Fees

Non-GAAP gross profit increased 18% year over year to $767.8 million. However, non-GAAP gross margin contracted 90 basis points year over year to 49.2%, primarily due to $53 million of incremental U.S. carrier pass-through fees. Excluding these fees, gross margin would have expanded 80 basis points.

Non-GAAP income from operations surged 39% year over year to $325.7 million. Non-GAAP operating margin expanded 290 basis points to approximately 21%, reflecting strong gross profit growth and cost efficiencies. Operating income benefited from approximately $11 million in platform credits.

Twilio's Cash Generation Remains Strong

Net cash provided by operating activities reached $389.2 million compared with $263.6 million in the prior-year quarter. Free cash flow increased approximately 49% year over year to $369.6 million, with a free cash flow margin of 24%, up from 19%.

Twilio ended the third quarter with $1.06 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $1.83 billion in short-term marketable securities. Long-term debt stood at $993.6 million. The company repurchased $127.2 million of shares during the quarter, leaving approximately $700 million under its existing authorization.

TWLO Raises Its 2026 Outlook

For 2026, Twilio raised its reported revenue growth outlook to 20% from 18-18.5% and its organic revenue growth projection to 15% from 13-13.5%. The company also increased its non-GAAP income from operations and free cash flow guidance to $1.19-$1.20 billion each compared with the previous range of $1.135-$1.155 billion.

For the fourth quarter of 2026, Twilio expects revenues between $1.595 billion and $1.605 billion, indicating reported growth of 17-17.5% and organic growth of 11-12%. Non-GAAP income from operations is projected at $300-$310 million, with non-GAAP earnings of $1.48-$1.53 per share.

Twilio Provides an Upbeat 2027 Preliminary Outlook

Management expects organic revenue growth of at least 10% in 2027, exceeding its earlier long-term framework of 7-8%. Non-GAAP gross profit growth is anticipated to remain broadly aligned with organic revenue growth.

Twilio also projects non-GAAP income from operations and free cash flow of at least $1.35 billion each in 2027.

news.Title: ASE Technology Q3 Earnings Beat Estimates on AI-Driven LEAP Growth
news.Content:
ASE Technology Holding ASX reported third-quarter 2026 earnings of 37 cents per ADS, which increased 125.3% year over year and beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 8.8%.

Revenues surged 44.8% year over year and 27.8% sequentially to NT$244.16 billion. In U.S. dollar terms, revenues of $7.64 billion surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 3.3%. Results reflected robust artificial intelligence (AI)-driven demand for Leading-edge Advanced Packaging (LEAP) services, with Assembly, Testing and Materials (ATM) revenues climbing 51% year over year.

ASX ATM Growth Accelerates on LEAP Demand

ATM revenues totaled NT$151.49 billion, up 20.1% sequentially and 51% year over year. Packaging revenues surged 52.5% to NT$122.95 billion, while testing revenues advanced 42.8% to NT$26.30 billion.

Management cited strong demand across LEAP and conventional semiconductor services, with capacity operating at or near full utilization. Faster-than-expected installations of LEAP capacity supported revenue growth, while demand continued to exceed available supply across advanced and mainstream packaging operations.

ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | ASE Technology Holding Co., Ltd. Quote

ASE Technology Revenue Mix Shifts Toward Computing

Computing represented 34% of ATM revenues, up from 25% in the year-ago quarter. Communication's contribution declined to 38% from 45%, while automotive, consumer and other applications accounted for 28%.

By service type, bumping, flip-chip, wafer-level packaging and system-in-package services contributed 51% of ATM revenues. Wire bonding accounted for 24%, testing represented 17%, other services contributed 6%, and materials made up 2%.

Management expects computing applications to remain a major growth driver through 2027 and 2028, supported by increasing LEAP adoption in high-performance computing and other advanced semiconductor applications.

ASE Technology's EMS Results Stay Mixed

Electronic Manufacturing Services (EMS) revenues increased 35.4% year over year and 42.1% sequentially to NT$93.47 billion. Consumer applications represented 41% of EMS revenues, computing contributed 21%, and communication accounted for 19%.

EMS gross margin declined 60 basis points sequentially to 8.3%, reflecting higher pass-through component costs and product-mix changes. However, operating margin improved to 3.3% from 2.4% in the prior quarter, supported by operating expense leverage.

Story Continues

Management noted that growing demand for AI accelerators contributed to computing revenue expansion, while elevated component costs continued to weigh on profitability.

ASE Technology Margins Expand

Consolidated gross profit increased 86.9% year over year to NT$53.97 billion. Gross margin expanded 500 basis points to 22.1%, reflecting stronger ATM revenues, favorable LEAP product mix and currency benefits.

Operating income surged 151% to NT$33.14 billion, while operating margin improved 580 basis points to 13.6%. Operating expenses increased to NT$20.82 billion, mainly due to higher headcount, profit-sharing expenses and research and development spending.

ATM gross margin reached 30.6%, up from 22.6% a year earlier, while operating margin expanded to 20% from 10.8%. Management indicated that increasing LEAP contributions have pushed profitability beyond the segment's previous structural margin ceiling.

ASX Investment Spending Moves Higher

Equipment capital expenditures totaled $2.10 billion during the third quarter, including $991 million for packaging operations, $1.07 billion for testing, $41 million for EMS and $5 million for interconnect materials and other activities.

The company additionally invested approximately $1.8 billion in facilities and land during the quarter. Management raised its 2026 capital expenditure budget to $11.5 billion from $10.5 billion, reflecting continued investment in semiconductor capacity expansion.

ASE Technology has 22 ongoing building projects in Taiwan, with more than half expected to begin supporting revenues by 2027. Management anticipates higher capital expenditures in 2027 as capacity constraints persist.

As of Sept. 30, 2026, ASE Technology held NT$107.94 billion in cash, cash equivalents and current financial assets. Total interest-bearing debt increased to NT$406.46 billion, while unused credit facilities totaled NT$457.28 billion. The net debt-to-equity ratio was 0.66.

Net cash generated from operating activities reached NT$50.46 billion during the quarter.

For the fourth quarter of 2026, management expects consolidated revenues to increase 6-8% sequentially in New Taiwan dollar terms. Gross margin is projected between 23% and 24%, while operating margin is expected in the 14.5-15.5% range. ATM revenues are forecast to grow 11-13% sequentially, with gross margin improving 100-200 basis points. EMS revenues are expected to remain relatively flat, with operating margin around 2%.

Management raised its 2026 LEAP revenue outlook to more than $4 billion and expects LEAP revenues to double in 2027. Full-process packaging revenues are projected to exceed $1 billion in 2027, while co-packaged optics revenues are expected to surpass $500 million, supported by sustained demand for advanced semiconductor technologies.

news.Title: SIMO Q3 Earnings Call Highlights AI and Enterprise Growth Outlook
news.Content:
Silicon Motion Technology Corporation SIMO outlined an ambitious growth outlook during its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, emphasizing expanding opportunities in enterprise storage, automotive applications and AI infrastructure.

Management expects revenue to grow at least 40% in 2027, supported by customer design wins, improving product mix and rising demand for specialized storage solutions, despite persistent weakness in consumer markets.

SIMO Projects Strong Growth Through 2027

Fourth-quarter revenues are expected between $588 million and $616 million, representing sequential growth of 5% to 10%. Non-GAAP gross margin is expected between 54% and 55%, with operating margin reaching 36% to 37%.

For 2027, revenue growth is expected to be at least 40%, with gross margins remaining in the low-to-mid-50% range. Management anticipates continued operating leverage as enterprise and automotive products contribute more revenue.

During the quarter, revenues reached $560 million, exceeding the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $532.8 million. Adjusted earnings of $4.35 per ADS surpassed the consensus estimate of $3.30.

Silicon Motion Technology Corporation Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Silicon Motion Technology Corporation price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Silicon Motion Technology Corporation Quote

Silicon Motion Sees Enterprise Storage Momentum

Chief executive officer Wallace Kou emphasized growing demand for MonTitan enterprise SSD controllers across NAND manufacturers, hyperscalers and cloud service providers.

All seven announced MonTitan customers remain on track for commercial production ramps during 2026. The company also completed tape-out of its next-generation 4nm PCIe Gen 6 controller, with sampling scheduled for the first quarter of 2027.

Management expects TLC-based enterprise SSD demand to lead near-term growth, while QLC-based storage opportunities expand as higher-density NAND becomes available. Kou expects broader adoption to strengthen MonTitan's contribution beyond 2026.

SIMO Expands Automotive and Boot Drive Opportunities

Kou highlighted Ferri automotive and enterprise boot drives as major growth engines. Combined solutions revenues increased more than 75% sequentially and represented over 40% of third-quarter sales.

Automotive products benefited from expanding customer relationships and higher margins. Management also identified opportunities in robotics, drones and advanced networking, although robotics demand remains at an early stage.

Enterprise boot drives represent another expansion opportunity. Kou expects the market for DRAM-equipped near-CPU boot drives to exceed $10 billion by 2030, with Silicon Motion targeting product ramps in the second half of 2027.

Story Continues

Silicon Motion Addresses Supply and Pricing Risks

During the analyst Q&A, B. Riley Securities questioned whether supply constraints could limit growth beyond management's 2027 expectations.

Kou responded that Silicon Motion has secured wafer capacity primarily through TSMC, alongside assembly, testing and substrate resources, to support its anticipated expansion.

William Blair analysts examined exposure to NAND pricing fluctuations. Kou explained that customer pricing arrangements generally span six months, helping manage costs. Chief financial officer Jason Tsai added that normalization of storage specifications and new customer programs could support growth even if NAND prices stabilize.

SIMO Details Funding and Consumer Market Pressures

Management acknowledged continuing weakness in smartphones and PCs as elevated memory prices pressure device affordability. Kou expects eMMC and UFS controller demand to remain relatively flat near term.

In contrast, PCIe Gen 5 controller adoption offers higher average selling prices and additional market share opportunities. Management expects the technology's PC market penetration to reach 20% to 25% by the end of 2027.

Responding to working-capital questions, Tsai said the company's $1.15 billion convertible-note financing should support anticipated funding requirements for the next couple of years. Inventory conversion remains an important consideration as solutions revenues expand.

Silicon Motion Focuses on More Diversified Growth

Management's overarching message centered on reducing dependence on consumer storage cycles through higher-value enterprise, automotive and AI applications.

Tsai emphasized that longer product lifecycles and multi-year customer engagements should improve business visibility. Management remains focused on scaling these opportunities while maintaining profitability and managing supply constraints.
